Nothing is deleted without a written request.

The estimate is built on one assumption, and here it is.

Eleven pages, one hour, and I read it three times. The first pass is for what is excluded, because that is where the money is, and it is usually one line in the middle of a paragraph. The second pass is the one nobody does. I mark every sentence that does not say who does the thing. The data is sent, access is granted, the file is validated. Every one of those will be assigned to somebody at signature, and if you did not ask, the somebody is you. The third pass is dates and dependencies, and I read those with a pen, because a date with nobody attached to it is not a date. One more thing, and I have made this mistake myself. Watch the word standard. Standard means standard for them, not standard for you, and it is the word I ask about more than any other.

Projects are almost never late because of the work. The work is usually estimated correctly, by people who have done it many times before. They are late because of something nobody wrote down. My favourite example, and I have seen it four times, is a firewall rule change on the customer side. It is twenty minutes of work and six weeks of waiting, because it sits between two teams and it is on nobody's list. That is a dependency, and if it is not in the document it does not exist. And then there is the sentence I hear at every unhappy meeting: the estimate was wrong. The estimate was not wrong. The assumption was. And the difference matters, because a wrong estimate is a mistake somebody has to apologise for, and a wrong assumption is a conversation both sides can have, as long as somebody had the courage to write it down at the beginning.
